title: Perkins: access to the throne justifies; 'I believe my sins remitted' is highest, often absent
source_text: CXIX. Similia docuimus apud Perkinsum haberi in pluribus ejus operibus. Nam actum illum fidei, quem immediate sequitur peccatoris justificatio, dicit esse accessum ad thronum gratiae, ut apprehenso ibidem Christo, inveniamus misericordiam apud Deum. Et postea tandem succedere quintum & summum fidei gradum, qui est specialis persuasio, qua promissiones Evangelicas quisque sibi applicat. Hunc autem fidei gradum summum & perfectissimum pertendit abesse a multis fidelibus, qui nequeunt distincte & certo de se dicere, credo ego remissionem peccatorum meorum. Quorum licet fides infirma sit, vere tamen sunt Dei filii, Et nihilominus eos divina misericordia non deficit, aut destituit. Adeoque Catechismos quosdam, qui fidem dicunt esse certam & plenam persuasionem de amore Dei & favore erga nos in Christo, fidem in summo & perfectissimo sui gradu definire.
pass_a_gloss: We have taught that similar things are found in Perkins in several of his works. For that act of faith which the sinner's justification immediately follows, he says is access to the throne of grace, that having apprehended Christ there we may find mercy with God. And afterward at last there succeeds the fifth and highest degree of faith, which is the special persuasion by which each applies the Gospel promises to himself. But this highest and most perfect degree of faith he contends is absent from many believers who cannot distinctly and certainly say of themselves, I believe the remission of my sins. Whose faith, though weak, yet they are truly sons of God, and nonetheless divine mercy does not fail or forsake them. And so certain Catechisms that say faith is a certain and full persuasion of God's love and favor toward us in Christ define faith in its highest and most perfect degree.
pass_b_english: Perkins: the faith-act justification immediately follows is access to the throne of grace to find mercy in Christ.
The fifth, highest degree — distinct 'I believe my sins are remitted' — is often missing in true children of God whom mercy does not forsake.
Catechisms that define faith as full persuasion of God's love toward us describe faith at its summit, not its essence.
